To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) industry funded studies were more likely than nonindustry funded studies to be published in high-impact journals and to report positive results, (2) the authors of industry funded studies were significantly more likely than those of nonindustry funded studies, to have financial ties to industry, and (3) the authors of studies that reported positive results were more likely than those that reported negative results to have financial ties with industry.

(1) 40% of all articles on the use of drugs or medical devices in _Mayo Clinical Proceedings_ from 1998 through 2003 were funded by industry, (2) industry-funded articles are 5 times more likely to have a favorable conclusion than articles that are not funded by industry, and (3) industry-funded articles were significantly more likely to report a conflict of interest than non-industry-funded articles.
the pharmaceutical industry is the primary funder of clinical trials and that industry-funded trials are less likely than nonindustry-funded trials to report favorable results.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are committed to the principles of transparency and integrity in scientific publications.
our policy is to disclose the contribution of all authors to the study, and that we are transparent about the contributions of others who may have been involved in writing the manuscript.
we are trying to eliminate ghostwriting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
industry funding is associated with a higher rate of ghost authorship, which may be a surrogate for other forms of conflict of interest, including authorship.
authors should not use professional writers without including them as authors and that journals should require disclosure of all contributions to the study and the manuscript.
industry-funded research is not a reliable source of information for clinicians.
